about:
Painted in Düsseldorf by a German-American who hoped it would stiffen the spines of Europe’s reformers after the failed revolutions of 1848. The scene is the night of December 25, 1776, when Washington crossed the icy Delaware to surprise the Hessian garrison at Trenton.

It is more than twenty-one feet wide. Almost every detail has been picked apart by historians, and none of that has dented it.

Painted in June 1889 at the asylum in Saint-Rémy, a few weeks after The Starry Night. Van Gogh thought the cypresses deserved the attention he had given sunflowers, and he counted this among his best summer landscapes.

Nothing in it holds still: the wheat, the olive trees and the clouds are all drawn with the same rolling stroke.

Sargent asked to paint Virginie Gautreau, a Louisiana-born Paris socialite famous for her looks, and hoped the picture would make his name. It did, the wrong way: at the 1884 Salon the pose and the pallor caused a scandal, made worse by a jewelled strap that he had painted slipping off her shoulder.

He repainted the strap, moved to London, and kept the canvas for more than thirty years before selling it to the Met, telling the director it was perhaps the best thing he had done.

A woman rests one hand on a window and the other on a silver pitcher, and that is the whole event. What Vermeer is really painting is daylight: how it comes through the glass, turns the linen cap blue, and lands on the wall.

It was the first Vermeer to enter an American collection, given to the Met in 1889.

One of six panels of the seasons that Bruegel painted for the Antwerp merchant Niclaes Jongelinck; five survive. This is late summer. Some people are cutting wheat, others are eating and sleeping under a pear tree, and the land runs downhill all the way to the sea.

It is often called the first modern landscape, because the religious pretext is gone and the people are simply working.

One of the first pure landscapes in Spanish painting. El Greco lived in Toledo for half his life and here rearranges it to suit himself, moving the cathedral beside the Alcázar and setting the whole city under a sky that looks about to break.

Two dozen dancers and their mothers wait while the ballet master Jules Perrot conducts an examination. The rehearsal room is in the old Paris Opéra, which had burned down the year before, so Degas built the scene from memory and drawings.

Look at the edges: a dancer scratching her back, a watering can, a small dog.

title: Under the Wave off Kanagawa (The Great Wave)
about:
The first print in the series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, designed when Hokusai was about seventy. Three boats row into the wave; Fuji sits small and still in the hollow beneath it.

The blue is Prussian blue, a synthetic pigment then newly imported into Japan, and part of why the series sold so well.

Rembrandt at fifty-four, a few years after his bankruptcy, looking at himself without flattery: the heavy brow, the soft cheeks, the thick paint in the face and almost none in the clothes. He painted himself some forty times, and this is among the plainest.

Monet dug the pond at Giverny, planted it, built the arched bridge, and then in the summer of 1899 sat down and painted the same view of it again and again. The water garden would be his subject for the rest of his life.

Prometheus, punished for giving fire to people, is chained to a rock while an eagle tears at his liver. Rubens painted the figure and his friend Frans Snyders, the animal specialist, painted the eagle. Rubens kept it in his own house for years and counted it among his best.
The Sacramento Valley after rain: cattle, oaks, and a storm moving off. Bierstadt painted it in his New York studio from sketches made in California a few years earlier.

about: A double rainbow over an Andean gorge, assembled from Church’s travels in Ecuador and Jamaica. He painted it the year after the Civil War ended and after losing two children to diphtheria, and it is usually read as a picture of hope after a disaster.

about: Monet went to Venice once, in the autumn of 1908, and said it was too beautiful to be painted. Then he painted thirty-seven canvases. This one looks across the Grand Canal to Santa Maria della Salute.
